extraction_notes.note: The constructions of the localizing cutoffs alpha_k and of the corner neighborhood U are procedures written in prose; typed as definitions (what they produce) rather than unmarked algorithms, since no computation is performed.

Statements that N_ballistic is a classical PsiDO of order -1 are applications of Lemma 2 of Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann to the paper's operator; emitted as paper claims rather than external theorems since the cited lemma itself is not stated.

Sections 4.1-4.3 are a long calculation chained through numbered displays with little prose; each numbered display is an equation node and the chain is recorded with uses edges between consecutive displays, while unnumbered displays stay inside the surrounding text.

The smoothness argument for the reflected kernel spans two paragraphs ending with 'Therefore, (34) is a smoothing integral operator.'; the last sentence was taken as the claim and the preceding paragraphs (including the definition of q_j, later reused) as its prose proof.
The same \label{forwardoperator} is attached to both equation (3) and equation (13); it is never referenced, so no edge depends on it. Figures are \input pdf_tex files not present in the source.

Prior results of Novikov, Bal, Eskin and Ilmavirta are only mentioned in the introduction, not stated, so they get no nodes; the even-part notation [g]_even, used only within one display, is also left in the text.

nodes.statement: Although this problem is relatively new in its consideration, there are some previously existing results which are somewhat related. In particular, Eskin proved a uniqueness result for C^infty unknown functions in 2-dimensions given knowledge of broken rays that reflect off of known convex obstacles in the domain's interior (). There the weight function is taken to be a smooth electric potential V(x). One of the main tools used in the proof is a differential identity of Mukhometov (), specific to two dimensions, which involves the integrals of the potential along broken rays. Furthermore, the recent work of Ilmavirta in proves an injectivity result on the disk for open subsets E of the boundary when the unknown function f is uniformly quasianalytic in the angular variable (when written in polar coordinates).

nodes.statement: Finally, we mention some recent work of Salo and Kenig, which provides explicit motivation for the consideration of such a broken ray transform in the first place (). There the authors consider the recovery of a Schr\"odinger potential on a particular class of compact manifolds from partial Cauchy data, deemed conformally transversally anisotropic. nodes.statement: Although general polyhedral domains lack obvious reflection rules at the corners (some authors ignore such trajectories and some define them in terms of limits of regular trajectories, e.g. ), the special symmetrical nature of the square does give an unambiguous rule for such reflections. But one still runs into the problem that the composite functions z_j(x,theta), theta_j(x,theta) are not real analytic for (x,theta) associated with a corner point. One simple, albeit more restrictive route, is to assume that the subset E also includes a small neighborhood of each corner. In that case, all broken rays with corner points are just ballistic X-rays. More generally, one can cut out the rays with corner points from the measurement operator. However, if one assumes the attenuation coefficient to vanish in a neighborhood of the boundary, it is still possible to treat rays with corners as we will discuss later.

\begin{equation*}
\int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta.
\end{equation*}
Now observe that
\begin{align*}
\| \alpha I_{\sigma, E} f(x,\theta) \|_{L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})}^{2} & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} |\alpha(x,\theta)|^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} [w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\

& = 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\
& = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\Gamma_{-}} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(x+t\theta,\theta)|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\
& = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})}^{2}.
\end{align*}

Now we consider the reflected hyperplane $P_{2}$, which we still denote with the same notation, and reflect the previously reflected copy of $\Omega$ across it.
